One winner per input row

Source: R/normalize_gazetteer.R
nar_gazetteer_winner.Rd

The highest-scoring reading; on a tie, the one that answered in the municipality the string wrote; and on a tie in that too, the earliest candidate – which is the baseline parse. A reading only displaces the baseline by resolving to a street this one does not, or to the same quality of street without moving the town.

The middle term is not a preference for tidiness. A municipality swap is normally fined 0.88, so a reading that moved the town rarely ties one that did not – but the fine exempts an *attested* swap, and an attested swap is exactly what a real place name buys: `170 North Park St, Brantford` resolves at 1.0 to `Park Rd N` in HAMILTON, because Brantford and Hamilton share a census subdivision name, while the reading that keeps the compass word in the name resolves at 1.0 to `North Park St` in Brantford itself. Two readings, both perfect, and the exemption is what let the wrong one through. Score cannot separate them and the swap penalty has already declined to, so the only remaining question is which one stayed where it was told.

It cannot fire on a row with one candidate, and it cannot fire where the string named no municipality – there `mun_kept` is `FALSE` for every reading of the row, since it compares against the *baseline* reading's municipality, which is the same value for all of them. That anchoring is also why the term is inert on the municipality-anchored variants: those exist to re-segment a trailing run into a town the baseline missed, so their answers are the ones that differ from the baseline's, and the term points back at the baseline they were generated to challenge. It bites in one place, which is the place it was measured on.

Usage

nar_gazetteer_winner(best)

Arguments

best

Scored rows carrying `.row`, `.cand`, `score` and `mun_kept`

Value

`best`, one row per `.row`
